newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-S&P says upgrades Philippines' foreign rating.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-S&P says upgrades Philippines' foreign rating.

text.p: Standard and Poor's Corp said on Friday it has raised its rating on US$4.4 billion of the Philippines' long term foreign currency debt to BB-plus from BB.
Also upgraded to BB-plus were National Power Corp, Philippine Long Distance Telphone Company (PLDT) and Bangko Sentra ng Pilipinas.
S&P said it also upgraded ratings on about US$10.7 billion of the Philippines' peso-denominated debt to A-minus and A-1, from BBB-plus and A-2 respectively.
The outlook on the long-term ratings remained positive, S&P said.
S&P said the upgrade of the Philippines' debt reflected improvements in public finances.
However, it said the ratings remained constrained by several factors, including the challenge of broadening the public sector's revenue base.
The ratings agency said broadening the revenue base would be essential to support adequate infrastructure development going forward and to reduce the share of non-discretionary expenses.
"Despite delays in implementing some reforms, the Ramos administration has kept spending pressures in check and brought the budget closer to balance," S&P said.
It said public sector debt and interest payments should decline to about 60 percent of gross domestic product and 20 percent of revenues in 1997 as a result.
S&P said financial flexibility would be enhanced longer term by Congress' expected approval of the remaining elements of the government's comprehensive tax reform package in coming months.
S&P said the rating was also supported by a rapidly diminishing foreign debt burden and increasingly favourable prospects for output and exports.

"Net public external debt, estimated at 41 percent of exports this year, is less than half its level of 1994," S&P said. "Total public and private sector debt service (including short term debt) has declined to about 35 percent of exports from 55 percent," it said. "Both ratios now compare favourably with those of other similarly rated sovereigns and are set to fall further on current trends," the ratings agency said.

S&P said that after a lacklustre performance for much of the decade, the trend rate of real GDP growth was about six percent annually and was still rising as a result of the ongoing impact of microeconomic reform.
"Foreign investment inflows, in turn, are now about US$2 billion annually, and export volumes are continuing to increase at double-digit rates," it said.

However, S&P also noted domestic savings and investment rates, estimated at 20 percent and 24 percent of GDP in 1997, which it said limited faster GDP growth and were notably lower than in other ASEAN countries.
The ratings agency also said external finances were also reliant on confidence-sensitive capital flows and worker remittances.

"A current account deficit of over four percent of GDP and central bank reserves of less than three months of imports, while manageable, underscore the importance of maintaining conservative fiscal and monetary policies."
It also noted "a political culture, especially in Congress, where powerful vested interests, patronage, and corruption can slow and dilute economic reforms."

The agency said a further improvement in the Philippines' credit standing depended on congressional approval of the tax reform package, achieving levels of tax adminstration that boost recurrent revenues significantly, success by the central bank in keeping inflation at single-digit rates and, with elections due in May 1998, evidence that the commitment to current economic policies will continue in the next administration.
